c.tagline: Rose City of food carts, craft beer, indie shops, and forested trails.

taxi.fareNote: Traditional taxis are metered, but ride-hailing (Uber/Lyft) is far more common and usually cheaper; street-hailing is rare outside downtown.

emergency.note: 911 is the single nationwide emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance across the US.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Caution in parts of downtown/Old Town — open drug use and property crime

hood_desc: The compact central core with Pioneer Courthouse Square, the waterfront, Powell's City of Books, and clusters of food carts; the MAX and streetcar hub and the easiest base for first-timers.
A converted-warehouse district of art galleries, design shops, breweries, and upscale lofts; polished, walkable, and known for First Thursday art walks and boutique shopping.
A colorful NE Portland strip of galleries, murals, indie shops, and eclectic eateries famous for its street fairs; artsy, offbeat, and quintessentially Portland.
A classically quirky SE Portland stretch of vintage stores, bookshops, food carts, and casual bars; laid-back, bohemian, and very walkable.
An upscale, tree-lined district along NW 23rd and 21st Avenues packed with boutiques, cafes, and restaurants in restored Victorians; prime for shopping and strolling.
lodging: The Nines, a Luxury Collection Hotel
Residence Inn by Marriott Portland Downtown/Pearl District

water.note: Tap water from the Bull Run watershed is excellent.

transit.hours: MAX and most buses run from around 4am to just past midnight, with reduced frequency in the evenings and on weekends.
transit.pay: Tap a Hop Fastpass card, contactless bank card, or phone at MAX and streetcar platforms and on buses. A 2.5-hour adult fare is $2.80 and a day pass is $5.60; Hop automatically caps your daily and monthly spending.

train: Union Station (Amtrak Cascades / Coast Starlight / Empire Builder)

transit.m: MAX Red Line to downtown (~40 min)

tip.r: ~15-20% at restaurants and bars is expected across the US; tipping is a core part of service workers' pay.

food.name: Food-cart pod fare
food.desc: Portland's defining meal: hundreds of permanently parked carts selling Thai, Lebanese, Korean, Mexican and vegan plates from tiny kitchens.

places.name: Cartopia
places.note: The classic late-night pod with poutine, pizza and Thai carts side by side.

places.name: Prost Marketplace
places.note: Carts ringing a beer-garden courtyard so everyone can order something different.

places.name: Nong's Khao Man Gai
places.note: Cart-born Thai chicken and rice that became a full Portland institution.

food.name: Portland doughnuts
food.desc: Two rival styles: Voodoo's gleefully absurd cereal-topped rings and Blue Star's brioche doughnuts filled with jam, curd and creme.

places.name: Voodoo Doughnut
places.note: The original pink-box shop; open late and still the tourist rite of passage.

places.name: Blue Star Donuts
places.note: Brioche-dough doughnuts made in small batches; sold out by mid-afternoon.

places.name: Doe Donuts
places.note: All-vegan shop that consistently outranks the big names with locals.

food.name: Dungeness crab
food.desc: Sweet Oregon coast crab served cracked and cold, in cakes or in a Louie salad; peak season runs from December into spring.

places.name: Jake's Famous Crawfish
places.note: Open since 1892; the benchmark Portland seafood house for crab and oysters.

places.name: Dan and Louis Oyster Bar
places.note: Family-run since 1907, with crab cocktails and stew in a nautical dining room.

places.name: Portland Farmers Market at PSU
places.note: Saturday market where coastal fishers sell whole cooked Dungeness in season.

food.name: Marionberry pie
food.desc: Deep-purple pie made from the marionberry, a blackberry bred in Oregon in the 1950s and grown almost nowhere else.

places.name: Random Order Coffeehouse and Bakery
places.note: Alberta staple whose fruit pies are the reason most people walk in.

places.name: Lauretta Jean's
places.note: All-butter crusts and Oregon berry fillings; also does a strong biscuit brunch.

places.name: Pacific Pie Company
places.note: Australian-style pie shop with a sweet counter of seasonal berry pies.

food.name: Pacific salmon and chanterelles
food.desc: Wild Chinook or coho from the Columbia paired with foraged Oregon chanterelles, hazelnuts and Willamette Valley vegetables.

places.name: Higgins Restaurant
places.note: Pioneer of Pacific Northwest farm-to-table cooking, running since 1994.

places.name: Ned Ludd
places.area: NE Martin Luther King Jr Blvd
places.note: Everything cooked in a wood-fired oven, menu driven by local foragers.

places.name: Andina
places.note: Peruvian kitchen that builds its ceviches and mains on Northwest seafood.

food.name: Farm-to-cone ice cream
food.desc: Small-batch scoops built on Oregon dairy and oddball local ingredients, from pear and blue cheese to honey lavender.

places.name: Salt and Straw
places.note: The shop that started the Portland ice cream boom; expect a line most evenings.

places.name: Salt and Straw
places.note: Second flagship in Nob Hill with the same rotating seasonal flavour board.

places.name: Fifty Licks
places.note: Quieter local favourite with a strong vegan coconut-base range.

food.name: Oregon craft beer
food.desc: Portland has more breweries than almost any US city; hazy IPAs, sour ales and cask bitters are all local house styles.

places.name: Cascade Brewing Barrel House
places.note: The temple of Northwest sour beer, aged in wine barrels with Oregon fruit.

places.name: Breakside Brewery
places.note: Repeat award winner whose IPAs define the modern Oregon style.

places.name: Deschutes Brewery Public House
places.note: Big, easy first stop with a wide range of Oregon classics on tap.

food.name: Third-wave coffee
food.desc: Portland roasts and pours some of America's most exacting coffee, from single-origin pour-overs to the cold brew style it helped popularise.

places.name: Stumptown Coffee Roasters
places.note: The roaster that put Portland coffee on the map, still the reference point.

places.name: Coava Coffee Roasters
places.note: Airy woodshop-shared space known for precise single-origin brewing.

places.name: Heart Coffee Roasters
places.note: Nordic-leaning light roasts and a minimalist bar locals rate highly.

landmarks: International Rose Test Garden
The oldest continuously operating public rose test garden in the US, with thousands of blooms and postcard views of Mount Hood.
Portlandia Statue
A giant hammered-copper statue kneeling above the entrance of the Portland Building, one of the most recognizable pieces of civic art in the city.
Pittock Mansion
A grand early-1900s French Renaissance-style chateau perched in the West Hills, famous for its sweeping views of downtown Portland and Mount Hood.
Vista Bridge (Portland)
An elegant 1926 steel arch bridge over a wooded canyon, one of Portland's most photographed and historically poignant structures.
Portland Japanese Garden
Widely regarded as one of the most authentic Japanese gardens outside Japan, offering serene, meticulously landscaped views year-round.
Multnomah Falls
A dramatic 620-foot waterfall just outside the city in the Columbia River Gorge, crossed by the iconic Benson Bridge and one of the most photographed sites in Oregon.
Tilikum Crossing
The largest car-free bridge in the US, a striking cable-stayed span over the Willamette River reserved for transit, bikes, and pedestrians.
Powell's City of Books
The world's largest independent bookstore, occupying an entire city block and a beloved literary landmark for Portlanders and visitors alike.
St. Johns Bridge
A soaring Gothic-style suspension bridge with cathedral-like towers, framed beautifully by Cathedral Park and the Willamette River below.
Keep Portland Weird Mural / Voodoo Doughnut
The whimsically decorated Voodoo Doughnut shop in Old Town, an offbeat cultural icon embodying Portland's quirky, independent spirit.

train.note: Everything uses Union Station at 800 NW 6th Avenue, a 15-minute walk from downtown and served by the MAX Yellow and Green lines. One Amtrak Cascades round trip a day runs right through to Vancouver, British Columbia without changing in Seattle, taking roughly 8 hours; the other Cascades departures work Portland-Seattle in about 3.5 hours, with two continuing south to Salem and Eugene. The Coast Starlight runs daily south to Sacramento and Los Angeles, and the Empire Builder heads east through the Columbia River Gorge to Spokane and Chicago. Southbound travellers from Canada now clear US border formalities at Vancouver's Pacific Central Station, which opened North America's first rail preclearance facility in June 2026; going north, Canadian officers check passports on arrival.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use the depot at 550 NW 6th Avenue next to Union Station, plus curbside stops nearby. FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/) and Greyhound (https://www.greyhound.com/) run the I-5 corridor to Seattle in 3-4 hours and on through Bellingham to Vancouver BC, usually with a change in Seattle. POINT (https://oregon-point.com/) is the state-supported intercity network, operating 365 days a year from Union Station to Astoria and the north coast, south to Salem and Eugene, and east to Bend and Ontario. Carry a passport for the Canadian border, where the coach waits until every passenger has been processed.

ferry.note: Portland lies 100 miles up the Columbia and Willamette rivers and has no scheduled passenger ferry; the long-proposed Frog Ferry commuter service was never launched. What sails from the downtown waterfront is sightseeing and dining cruises, plus multi-day river cruises up the Columbia and Snake rivers towards Clarkston, Washington. For genuine ferries you need the Puget Sound network around Seattle, roughly three hours north.

half.name: Hood River
half.blurb: Columbia River Gorge town about an hour east is known for windsurfing, fruit orchards and a historic downtown of brick storefronts.

half.name: Mount Hood
half.blurb: Cascade volcano about 90 minutes east offers hiking around Timberline Lodge and views over glacier-fed rivers and alpine meadows.

half.name: Cannon Beach
half.blurb: Oregon coast town about 90 minutes west centers on Haystack Rock, a 235-foot sea stack rising from the sand.

half.name: Willamette Valley
half.blurb: Wine region south of the city, about 45 minutes away, holds rolling vineyards producing much of Oregon's pinot noir.

full.name: Mount St. Helens
full.blurb: Volcano in Washington state, about two and a half hours north, still shows the blast zone from its 1980 eruption.
